title: Wisdom Pitches Her Tent in Israel
sum: Wisdom stands up in the assembly of the Most High and praises herself. She came out of God's mouth, covered the earth like a mist, lived in the heights with her throne in the pillar of cloud, and walked the sky and the deep. She had a share in every nation, but she looked for one place to rest, and her Creator told her, "Pitch your tent in Jacob." So she served in the holy tent, settled in Zion and Jerusalem, and grew there like the land's finest trees and smelled like the temple's incense. She invites all who long for her to come and eat (24:19–22).

Then Ben Sira says in his own voice who she is: "the book of the covenant of God Most High, the law Moses commanded" (24:23). The law overflows with wisdom like the rivers of Eden, and no one, first or last, has ever finished studying it. The chapter ends with the teacher himself, whose small canal from Wisdom's river grew into a sea. This is the central poem of Sirach, and one of the passages behind the opening of John's Gospel.
readings: Read as Jewish wisdom

Ben Sira tells the story of Israel as Wisdom's story: she comes from God, seeks a home among the nations, and is given one in Israel, in the tent of the wilderness and then the temple in Jerusalem. He then names her: Wisdom is the Torah. On this reading, the chapter tells Jewish students that they do not need to look to other peoples for wisdom, because God has already placed it in their own law and worship.
Read as a picture of Christ

Christian readers have heard in Wisdom who comes from God's mouth, exists from the beginning and pitches her tent in Israel a picture of the Son, "the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24), the Word who "became flesh and pitched his tent among us" (John 1:14). On this reading the law of 24:23 is a stage on the way: what Ben Sira saw in the Torah, the New Testament sees fully in Jesus, who also says, "Come to me" (Matthew 11:28).
Read of Mary in the liturgy

Catholic liturgy has also applied the poem to Mary, the place where God's Wisdom came to dwell. The Catechism says that "the Church's Tradition has often read the most beautiful texts on wisdom in relation to Mary" (721); its footnote to that sentence names Sirach 24. This is a use of the text in worship, not a claim that Ben Sira was thinking of Mary.

views.C: The Catholic Lectionary for Mass reads 24:1–2, 8–12 on the Second Sunday after Christmas, beside the prologue of John, and 24:1, 3–4, 8–12, 19–21 in the Common of the Blessed Virgin Mary under the heading "Mary, seat of Wisdom". The Catechism, saying that the Church's Tradition has often read the most beautiful texts on wisdom "in relation to Mary", gives "Cf. Prov 8:1–9:6; Sir 24" in its footnote (Catechism 721, note 101). The traditional Latin Missal reads the Latin of this chapter (Vulgate 24:14–16, Greek 24:9–12) in a Mass of the Virgin Mary, Salve, sancta Parens (see the note at 24:9), and Catholic devotion took "mother of beautiful love" (24:18) as a title of Mary.
views.O: The Orthodox churches read Sirach in Greek, the form translated here, and so number its verses as this page does.
views.P: For Protestants, Sirach is not Scripture: Article VI of the Church of England has it read "for example of life and instruction of manners" but not "to establish any doctrine", and the Westminster Confession counts the Apocrypha among "other human writings". Even so, the Revised Common Lectionary, used by many Protestant churches, lists Sirach 24:1–12 among the readings for the Second Sunday after Christmas, with John 1. Protestant scholars read chapter 24 closely as a witness to the Jewish picture of Wisdom that lies behind John 1:1–14 and Matthew 11:28–30.
views.H: Historians read the poem as modeled on Proverbs 8 and on Israel's story of the wilderness tent and the temple, written by a Jerusalem teacher in the time of the high priest Simon (chapter 50). Read in its time, it can be heard as an answer to the Greek culture spreading through Judea: the wisdom that thinkers of the age sought everywhere has its true home in the Jewish law. The rivers and trees draw on Genesis 2 and on the land of Israel itself.
views.J: For Jewish readers the poem's point is plain: Wisdom is the Torah, given to Israel and living in its worship. Sirach is not in the Jewish Bible, and no Hebrew copy of this chapter has been found, but the idea that God's wisdom and the Torah are one is basic to later Jewish teaching.

deep.b:
The chapter has a clear shape. An introduction (24:1–2) gives Wisdom the floor. In 24:3–7 she tells where she came from and how she searched: from God's mouth, over the earth, through the heights, the sky and the deep, among all nations, looking for rest. In 24:8–12 God gives her a home in Jacob, and she serves in the tent and settles in Zion. In 24:13–17 she grows like trees and smells like incense, and in 24:19–22 she calls out an invitation. Then Ben Sira speaks (24:23–29): all this is the law, which overflows like the rivers of paradise. Last, the teacher speaks of himself (24:30–34).

Three words tie the poem together: "tent" (24:4, 8, 10, 15), "rest" (24:7, 8, 11) and "inheritance" (24:7, 8, 12, 20, 23). The Plain keeps each of them the same so the reader can follow the thread.

Ben Sira answers the question himself: "All these things are the book of the covenant of God Most High, the law Moses commanded" (24:23). For him Wisdom is God's own wisdom, created before all things (24:9), made present to Israel in the Torah. Baruch says the same (Baruch 4:1).

Christian readers have added two further readings. Because the New Testament calls Christ "the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24) and says the Word "pitched his tent among us" (John 1:14), many read Wisdom here as a picture of the Son. Because Mary is the one in whom that Word took flesh, Catholic liturgy has also read the poem of her. The two Christian readings do not replace Ben Sira's own; they read his poem in the light of what Christians believe came later. Protestants, who do not hold the book as Scripture, read it mainly as background to the New Testament.

settings.what: Wisdom's song in praise of herself
settings.by: Wisdom, speaking in a poem by Ben Sira
settings.to: inside the poem, the assembly of the Most High and her own people Israel (24:1–2); outside it, Ben Sira's students
settings.when: no occasion is named; the poem opens the second half of the book
settings.why: To tell young Jews where real wisdom is: not out among the nations, where Wisdom found no resting place, but in Israel's tent, Zion and temple. Her invitation (24:19–22) asks the students to come and keep coming, because her food leaves them hungry for more.
settings.readers: Ben Sira's students in Jerusalem, in the generation of the high priest Simon whom he praises in chapter 50; then Greek-speaking Jews who read his grandson's translation in Egypt. No Hebrew copy of this chapter has been found, so later readers knew it through the Greek and the Latin, in the churches.

settings.what: Ben Sira's key: Wisdom is the law
settings.by: Ben Sira, in his own voice
settings.why: To name the Wisdom of the poem as the law of Moses, quoting Deuteronomy 33:4, and to say that the law is as rich as the rivers of Eden: no student, first or last, will ever reach the end of it.

settings.what: The teacher speaks of his own work
settings.to: his students and all later readers ("for everyone who searches for her")
settings.when: at the close of the poem
settings.why: To place himself as a servant of Wisdom: his teaching is a canal from her river that grew beyond his plans. He offers it to every generation, which is how his grandson later explained translating the book.

title: Ten Happy Men and an Evil Wife
sum: The chapter opens with number sayings: three things that make life lovely (brothers who agree, neighbors who are friends, a husband and wife who get along), three kinds of people Ben Sira hates, and the beauty of wisdom in the old. Then come ten happy things, ending at the top: no one ranks above the one who fears the Lord (25:7–11).

From 25:13 to 25:26 Ben Sira turns to the evil wife: worse than a lion and a dragon, a sandy climb for an old man, a source of shame and gloom. In the middle of the poem stands 25:24, "The beginning of sin is from a woman, and on account of her we all die," one of the most debated lines in the book. The chapter ends with advice to divorce a wife who will not be guided.
readings: Read as a teacher's advice to young husbands

Ben Sira speaks to young men about to marry or newly married, in a world where marriage decided a man's happiness, health and good name. The evil wife of 25:13–26 is the opposite of the good wife of 26:1–4: both poems are about choosing well. On this reading 25:24 too is about marriage: a bad wife leads her husband into sin and an early death.
Read beside Genesis 3

Many readers, ancient and modern, hear in 25:24 the story of Eve, who took the fruit first. On this reading Ben Sira steps out of his marriage advice for one line to name where sin and death began, and lays it on the first woman. The chapter page's deep section weighs both readings and sets them beside Genesis and Paul.

views.C: The Catholic Church reads Sirach as Scripture, and Vatican II asks interpreters to look for "what meaning the sacred writers really intended" and to attend to the literary forms of the writer's time, "in accordance with the situation of his own time and culture" (Dei Verbum 12). On the origin of sin, the Catechism follows Paul: "All men are implicated in Adam's sin" (Catechism 402, on Romans 5:12). Neither document comments on 25:24 itself.
views.P: Protestants, who do not count Sirach as Scripture, read 25:24 beside Romans 5:12, where sin entered the world "through one man", and take Paul's word as the Bible's teaching.
views.H: Historians read the poem as part of a long ancient tradition of sayings about good and bad wives, written by a man for men. On 25:24 they are divided between the Eve reading and the bad-wife reading, which Bullard and Hatton report from Jack Levison and accept.
views.J: These chapters were valued by Jewish readers. The Cairo Genizah's Manuscript C, a Hebrew collection of sayings from Ben Sira, has 25:7–8, 25:13 (broken), 25:17–24, 26:1–3, 26:13 and 26:15–17, and the Talmud quotes the sayings on bad and good wives in Ben Sira's name (Yevamot 63b; Sanhedrin 100b).

deep.b:
The text. The Greek reads, word for word, "From a woman (gynē) beginning of sin, and through her we die, all." The first line has no verb, so it does not say whether it speaks of one event long ago or of something that happens again and again; the Plain says "is" so as not to decide. The Hebrew survives in Manuscript C from the Cairo Genizah (folio VII verso): me'ishah techillat 'avon, uvighlalah gava'nu yachad, which Parker and Abegg render "From a woman iniquity had its beginning and on account of her we perish together." The two agree in sense. The Plain gives the line plainly, without softening it.

Eve. The usual reading takes the woman as Eve (Genesis 3:6) and the death as the death of all people (Genesis 3:19). Read so, the line goes beyond Genesis, which holds the man and the woman both to account (Genesis 3:12–19), and differs from Paul, who says "sin entered the world through one man" (Romans 5:12). Christian teaching on original sin follows Paul.

The bad wife. Bullard and Hatton, in their handbook for translators, report that Jack Levison argues the line belongs to its poem (25:13–26): "woman" is a wife, "we" are husbands, and the death is a husband's early grave, the opposite of the good wife who doubles a man's days (26:1). They find his argument convincing. The Greek and Hebrew words for woman and wife are the same, so the text allows both readings.

Why it matters. If read of Eve, the verse lays sin and death on the first woman alone, and readers today often meet it in discussions of how Jewish and Christian writers have spoken about women. If read of a bad wife, it is a hard proverb about marriage. Either way the reader should know what the verse says and what Genesis and Paul say beside it.

echoes: Proverbs 16:31; Proverbs 20:29; Proverbs 21:9; Proverbs 21:19; Proverbs 24:17; Proverbs 30:15–31; Psalm 133:1; Deuteronomy 22:10; Deuteronomy 24:1; Genesis 2:24; Genesis 3:6–19; Romans 5:12; 1 Timothy 2:13–14; Wisdom of Solomon 2:24; Malachi 2:16; Matthew 19:3–9

settings.what: Number sayings and the ten happy things
settings.to: his students, young men of Jerusalem
settings.when: in the course of his teaching
settings.why: To show what makes a life good and what spoils it, and to lift the list to its peak: wisdom is great, but the fear of the Lord is greater. The counting form helped students remember.
settings.readers: Proverbs-style lists like these were made to be learned by heart. The Hebrew of 25:7–8 survives in Manuscript C, a medieval Jewish collection of Ben Sira's sayings.

settings.to: young men who are married or about to marry
settings.when: no occasion is named; it is paired with the poem on the good wife in 26:1–4 and 26:13–18
settings.why: To warn students how much a bad marriage can ruin a man: his health, his peace, his standing among neighbors. The poem speaks only from the husband's side, as the teacher's audience was men. Readers today should know that it describes one side of a marriage in one culture, and that the same teacher praises a good wife as the Lord's gift.
settings.readers: The Talmud quotes the related sayings on bad and good wives in Ben Sira's name (Yevamot 63b; Sanhedrin 100b), and Manuscript C has parts of this poem in Hebrew (25:13, broken, and 25:17–24): these sayings were among the most remembered parts of the book in Jewish circles.

title: The Good Wife, and Lines Only in the Longer Greek
sum: Chapter 26 begins with praise of the good wife: the man who has one is happy, a wife of strength cheers her husband, and she is the Lord's gift to those who fear him. Then come three public fears and a fourth at home (a jealous rival wife), more warnings about a bad or drunken wife, and a hard passage on guarding a daughter (26:10–12). The poem on the good wife returns in 26:13–18, with pictures from the temple: the rising sun, the holy lampstand, golden pillars on silver bases.

Verses 19–27 are not in the great Greek codices or the Latin. They come from the longer form of the Greek, found in codex 248 and a few other manuscripts, which the KJV follows, and the Plain gives them in brackets. The chapter ends with things that anger Ben Sira and with a warning that merchants can hardly stay honest.
readings: Read in its own world

Ben Sira writes as a father and teacher of young men in a society where a family's honor rested on its women's conduct, where a man might have two wives, and where daughters were married off by their fathers. His praise of the good wife is warm; his warnings are harsh. Read in that world, the chapter is advice on choosing and keeping a household well.
Read beside the rest of the Bible

Readers who set the chapter beside Proverbs 31, the Song of Songs and the New Testament find both agreement and difference: the same high praise of a good wife (Proverbs 31:10–31), but little of the mutual love of the Song or Paul's "Husbands, love your wives" (Ephesians 5:25), and much more suspicion of women. Churches that hold the book as Scripture read such lines as a human author's teaching in his culture, to be weighed with the whole Bible.

views.C: For Catholic readers the chapter is Scripture, read as Vatican II asks: attending to "contemporary literary forms in accordance with the situation of his own time and culture" (Dei Verbum 12). Its praise of the good wife stands with Proverbs 31; its harsh lines are read in their setting and beside the New Testament.
views.P: Protestants read the chapter as Jewish wisdom outside Scripture, in Article VI's words "for example of life and instruction of manners", and weigh its counsel on marriage against the New Testament (Ephesians 5:25; 1 Peter 3:7).
views.H: Historians read 26:1–18 as part of a larger set of good-wife and bad-wife sayings (25:13–26:18), and 26:19–27 as a later addition found only in the longer Greek (codex 248, minuscule 70 and the Syriac, as Hart reports), not in the great codices or the Latin. The Hebrew of Manuscript C survives for 26:1–3, 13 and 15–17.
views.J: The Talmud quotes 26:1 and 26:3 in Ben Sira's name as sayings worth teaching even in public (Sanhedrin 100b; Yevamot 63b).

deep.b:
These chapters hold both warm and harsh words about women. The good wife doubles a man's days (26:1), is the Lord's gift (26:14), and shines like the sun in the sky and the lamp in the temple (26:16–17). The evil wife is worse than a lion and a dragon (25:16), and a daughter must be watched without letup (26:10–12). The site's Plain gives both as they stand.

Three things help a reader. First, the audience: Ben Sira teaches young men, so he speaks of women only as wives and daughters of men. Second, the setting: in his world a family's honor and property depended on its women's conduct, and a man could take a second wife (26:6). Third, the rest of the Bible: Proverbs shares much of this outlook (Proverbs 21:9; Proverbs 31:10–31), while the New Testament adds a call to mutual love and honor (Ephesians 5:25; 1 Peter 3:7). Readers differ on how much of Ben Sira's view is his culture and how much his own; the text itself should not be softened to settle that.

echoes: Proverbs 12:4; Proverbs 18:22; Proverbs 19:14; Proverbs 31:10–31; Proverbs 5:15–20; Proverbs 6:25; 1 Samuel 1:6; Leviticus 18:18; Deuteronomy 22:10; Exodus 25:31; Exodus 26:19; Ezekiel 18:24; Amos 8:5; 1 Peter 3:4; 2 Corinthians 6:14

settings.when: right after the poem on the evil wife
settings.why: To give the other side: a good wife is a man's greatest blessing and the Lord's gift to those who fear him. Pairing the two poems teaches a young man what to look for.
settings.readers: The Talmud quotes 26:1 and 26:3 (Sanhedrin 100b; Yevamot 63b), and Manuscript C copies them in Hebrew.

settings.what: Fears, the jealous wife, and the watched daughter
settings.to: his students as future husbands and fathers
settings.why: To warn of dangers in public life (slander, mobs, false charges) and at home (a rival wife, a drunken wife, a daughter left unguarded). The advice on daughters speaks to fathers responsible, in that society, for a daughter's marriage and good name.

settings.what: The beauty of a good wife
settings.why: To end on praise, with pictures taken from the sky and the temple: a good wife is to her home what the sun is to the heavens and the lamp to the sanctuary.

settings.by: an unknown writer; the lines are found in codex 248, minuscule 70 and the Syriac
settings.to: a "child", a young man, as in the rest of the book
settings.when: unknown: the lines are not in the great codices or the Latin
settings.why: To urge a young man to stay faithful, marry a good woman and raise children of a good name, and to contrast kinds of women in short pairs.
settings.readers: Readers of the Greek manuscripts and the Syriac that have these lines, and English readers of the KJV, which prints them as 26:19–27.

settings.what: Two things and a third; the merchant
settings.why: To name what angers him most (a righteous man who goes back to sin) and to warn that trade puts honesty at risk, leading into chapter 27.

title: Tested by Talk
sum: Ben Sira begins with the market: many sin for gain, and sin is jammed into buying and selling like a peg between stones. Then he tests people by their speech: the sieve keeps the rubbish, the furnace tests the potter's jars, the fruit shows how a tree was tended, and a person's words show the thoughts of his heart. Do not praise anyone until you have heard him reason (27:4–7).

Next come sayings on truth and sin, fools' talk and oaths, then a short poem on betraying a friend's secrets, which ends a friendship for good (27:16–21). The chapter closes with the man who winks and flatters, the evil that rolls back on its doer ("The one who digs a pit falls into it"), and the first line of a passage on anger and forgiveness that runs into chapter 28.
readings: Read as practical wisdom

These are proverbs for daily life in a city of shops and courts: be honest in business, judge people by their words, keep secrets, beware flatterers, and trust that wrongdoing comes back on the wrongdoer.
Read beside the Gospels

Several sayings sound like Jesus' teaching: the tree known by its fruit (Matthew 7:16–20; Matthew 12:33–34), the warning against swearing (Matthew 5:33–37), and anger as a sin (Matthew 5:22). They show how much of Jesus' teaching shared the wisdom of Jewish teachers before him, which he deepened and applied to the coming of God's kingdom.

views.C: Catholic readers read these sayings as part of the Church's moral wisdom, and the Latin text, which differs in several lines (27:1, 27:12), shaped how they were long heard.
views.P: For Protestants these are Jewish proverbs, useful "for example of life" (Article VI), which sit close to Proverbs and to the sayings of Jesus.
views.H: Historians read 27:1–7 as the outlook of a scribe who valued careful speech and was wary of trade, and note that several sayings (27:6, 27:26) are close to Proverbs and to Jesus' teaching.
views.J: The warnings about tale-bearing match the later Jewish teaching on lashon hara, evil speech, which the Talmud treats at length (Arakhin 15b).

echoes: Proverbs 11:1; Proverbs 11:13; Proverbs 17:3; Proverbs 20:19; Proverbs 6:13; Proverbs 10:10; Proverbs 26:27; Ecclesiastes 10:8; Psalm 7:15; Amos 8:5; Genesis 4:7; Matthew 5:22; Matthew 5:34–37; Matthew 7:16–20; Matthew 12:33–34; James 1:6–8; James 5:12; 1 Peter 5:8

settings.to: his students, some of whom would enter trade
settings.why: To warn that trade is full of small dishonesties and that only the fear of the Lord keeps a merchant's house standing.
To teach young men to judge others, and themselves, by speech: reasoning shows character as the furnace shows a jar.
To show how final the loss is when a friend's secret is given away: a wound heals and an insult can be patched up, but trust once betrayed does not come back.

settings.what: The flatterer and the evil that returns
settings.why: To warn of two-faced people and to assure the student that wrongdoing traps the wrongdoer, as Proverbs and the psalms say.

To teach that a person who holds on to anger cannot ask God for mercy: forgive your neighbor, and your own sins will be released when you pray. Remembering death and the commandments is the reason to let go.
settings.readers: Christian readers have long set 28:2 beside the Lord's Prayer (Matthew 6:12); the saying shows that Jesus' link between forgiving and being forgiven was already at home in Jewish teaching.

title: Forgive, and Guard Your Tongue
sum: The chapter opens with the clearest teaching on forgiveness in the book. The one who takes revenge will meet the Lord's revenge. "Forgive the wrong your neighbor did to you, and then, when you pray, your own sins will be released" (28:2). How can a man who keeps up anger against another ask God for healing? Remember death and the commandments, and let mistakes go.

The rest of the chapter is about quarrels and the tongue. Fights grow like fire with fuel; the same mouth can blow on a spark or spit it out (28:12). Then comes a long poem on "the tongue of a third party", slander, which has ruined cities, driven good wives out of their homes and killed more people than the sword. Ben Sira ends: weigh your words, and put a door and a bar on your mouth.
readings: Read as Jewish ethics

Forgiving others as a condition of being forgiven, and guarding the tongue, are two pillars of later Jewish ethics too. The Talmud's saying that "third speech" kills three (Arakhin 15b) is the same teaching as 28:13–23.
Read beside the Lord's Prayer and James

Christian readers hear 28:2 in the Lord's Prayer, "forgive us the debts we owe, just as we ourselves have forgiven" (Matthew 6:12), and 28:12–23 in James' warning that the tongue is a fire (James 3:5–10). Ben Sira gives the wisdom; Jesus grounds it in the Father's mercy first shown to us (Matthew 18:23–35).

views.C: In Catholic reading the chapter's teaching on forgiveness and speech fits the Church's moral teaching on mercy and on sins of the tongue. The Latin "Remember thy last things" (28:6) can be heard of the four last things: death, judgment, heaven and hell.
views.P: Protestant readers value 28:1–7 as a close pre-Christian parallel to the Lord's Prayer, while holding that forgiveness rests on Christ's work, not on forgiving others first.
views.H: Historians note that the phrase "third tongue" (28:14) makes little sense in Greek and probably carries over a Hebrew idiom, and readers often set 28:1–7 beside the teaching of Jesus.
views.J: The Talmud preserves a saying from the land of Israel: "Third speech... kills three people" (Arakhin 15b). Ben Sira's "third tongue" probably renders the same Hebrew idiom for slander.

deep.h: Ben Sira and Jesus on forgiveness
deep.b:
Ben Sira argues from fairness and from humility: a man who is "only flesh" (28:5) and needs mercy cannot refuse it to "a man like himself" (28:4). Jesus teaches the same link in the Lord's Prayer and adds, "If you do not forgive people, then neither will your Father forgive your wrongs" (Matthew 6:15). But Jesus also tells the parable of the slave who was forgiven a huge debt and then would not forgive a small one: "My heavenly Father will do the same to you, unless each one of you forgives his brother from the heart" (Matthew 18:35). In the parable, the king's mercy comes first, and the slave's duty to forgive flows from it.

So the two agree that an unforgiving person cannot expect forgiveness. They differ in what comes first: Ben Sira asks the student to forgive so that his prayer will be heard; Jesus tells his followers that they have already been forgiven much. Christians of every tradition read both sides of this in the Gospels.

echoes: Leviticus 19:17–18; Deuteronomy 32:35; Matthew 6:12–15; Matthew 18:21–35; Mark 11:25; Romans 12:19; Psalm 41:4; James 3:5–10; Proverbs 26:20–21; Proverbs 25:15; Psalm 141:3; Proverbs 21:23; Jeremiah 28:13–14; Isaiah 66:24; Mark 9:48

settings.why: To show how quarrels grow, and that each person can choose to feed or put out the fire with the same mouth.

settings.to: his students, future leaders of households and of the city
settings.why: To show what slander does: it breaks up peaceful families, brings down cities and great houses, and drives out good wives. Those who fear the Lord are sheltered from it; those who abandon him fall into it. The student must guard his words as he guards his money.

title: Lending, Alms and a Roof of Your Own
sum: Ben Sira turns to money between neighbors. Lending to a neighbor in need is mercy and keeps the commandments; borrowers should pay back on time. But he paints the borrower who kisses the lender's hand until he has the money, then makes excuses and treats the loan as a lucky find, so that many people stop lending at all (29:1–7).

Even so, be patient with the poor, give alms for the commandment's sake, and lose money for a brother rather than let it rust under a stone. "Store up your treasure as the Most High commands": alms will fight for you better than a shield (29:8–13). Standing good for a neighbor is what a good man does, but it has ruined many (29:14–20). The chapter ends with the life of a man who has no home of his own: better a poor roof than rich meals as a lodger who is ordered about and sent away (29:21–28).
readings: Read as a teacher's advice on money

Ben Sira is neither for nor against money. He asks for generosity (lend, give, stand good for a neighbor) and for prudence (do not ruin yourself, keep your independence). His students were the sons of families who had money to lend and needed to learn both.
Read beside Jesus' teaching

Jesus takes up the same themes and pushes them further: "lending without hoping for anything back" (Luke 6:35), treasure in heaven through giving to the poor (Matthew 6:19–21; Matthew 19:21), and a warning against seeking the best place at table (Luke 14:7–11). Ben Sira's alms as a treasure that rescues (29:12) is one of the passages behind the long debate among Christians about almsgiving and merit.

views.C: In Catholic reading, 29:8–13 belongs with Tobit 12:9 among the Scriptures on almsgiving. The "Where Christians differ" card at Tobit 4 sets out the Catholic and other views and is not repeated here.
views.P: Protestant readers welcome Ben Sira's call to generosity; how alms relate to forgiveness is a question on which they differ from Catholic teaching, set out on the card at Tobit 4.
views.H: Historians read the chapter as evidence for credit, guarantees and dependent "lodgers" in Jerusalem in Ben Sira's day, and note that Ben Sira mixes the Torah's duty to lend (Deuteronomy 15) with a hard-headed view of how loans go wrong.
views.J: Later Jewish teaching on tsedakah, charity, carries the same thought: giving to the poor is a deed God remembers. Ben Sira and Tobit are early witnesses to it.

echoes: Deuteronomy 15:7–11; Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:35–37; Psalm 37:21; Psalm 37:26; Proverbs 19:17; Proverbs 6:1–5; Proverbs 11:15; Proverbs 17:18; Proverbs 22:26; Proverbs 15:17; Proverbs 17:1; Genesis 43:9; Tobit 4:7–11; Tobit 12:8–9; Daniel 4:27; Matthew 6:19–21; Matthew 19:21; Luke 6:34–35; Luke 12:33; Luke 14:7–11; James 5:2–3; Hebrews 7:22; 1 Timothy 6:8

settings.to: students from families with money to lend
settings.why: To keep the Law's command to lend to a neighbor in need (Deuteronomy 15:7–11) alive in a world where borrowers often cheated lenders, and to tell borrowers to repay.
To urge generosity to the poor for the commandment's sake, with the promise that alms protect the giver. The question of merit this raises is set out at Tobit 4.

settings.what: On standing good for a neighbor
settings.why: To balance Proverbs' warnings: a good man helps a neighbor by guaranteeing his debt, but it has ruined many, so help "as far as you are able".
To warn young men against living off others: a poor roof of your own is better than a rich table where you must serve, take orders and leave when someone more honored arrives.
